nameStory: The red-bellied woodpecker gets its name from the subtle reddish wash on its lower belly and underparts, though this feature is often hard to spot in the field. It's a bit of a misleading name since the bird's most obvious red feature is actually its bright orange-red cap on the head! Many people think it should have been called the 'red-headed woodpecker,' but that name was already taken by a completely different species.
description: The red-bellied woodpecker is a medium-sized woodpecker about the size of a robin, with striking black-and-white barred patterns across its back and wings that look like zebra stripes. Both males and females sport bright orange-red caps, though males have red extending further down the back of their necks. Their bellies are grayish-white with just a hint of peachy-red coloring, and their faces and throats are clean gray. These adaptable birds have become increasingly common in New England as they expand their range northward.

idTips.label: Zebra-striped back
idTips.description: Bold black and white horizontal bars across the back and wings create an unmistakable ladder-like pattern that flashes as the bird moves

idTips.label: Orange-red cap
idTips.description: Bright rusty-orange to red coloring covers the top of the head; males have red extending down the nape while females have red only on top

idTips.label: Gray face and throat
idTips.description: Clean, pale gray coloring on the face and throat contrasts sharply with the red cap above

idTips.label: Rolling call
idTips.description: Gives a distinctive rolling 'churr' or 'kwirr' call that sounds softer and more musical than other woodpeckers' harsh calls

idTips.label: Subtle reddish belly
idTips.description: Faint peachy-red or pinkish wash on the lower belly and undertail area, often difficult to see except in good light

habitat: Red-bellied woodpeckers thrive in mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially areas with plenty of oak, hickory, and maple trees. They're equally at home in suburban neighborhoods with large shade trees, parks, and wooded residential areas. Look for them in areas where dead trees or snags are left standing, as these provide crucial nesting and foraging sites.

seasonality.spring: Active at nest cavities in dead trees, with loud drumming and calling as they establish territories and attract mates. Both parents take turns excavating nest holes.
seasonality.summer: Busy feeding young with frequent trips to and from nest holes. Adults may appear worn and less vibrant as they focus energy on raising their broods.
seasonality.fall: Highly active storing nuts and acorns in bark crevices for winter, often seen jamming food items into tree bark like living hammers.
seasonality.winter: Regular visitors to suet feeders and bird feeding stations, often the most reliable time to observe them closely as they become bolder around human activity.

funFact: Red-bellied woodpeckers are nature's ultimate food hoarders — they wedge thousands of acorns and nuts into bark crevices, fence posts, and even house siding, creating scattered pantries they remember and return to all winter long, sometimes stealing from other birds' caches too!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the red-headed woodpecker, which has a completely red head and neck (not just a cap), solid black back (not striped), and bright white belly. Remember: red-bellied has a striped back like a zebra, while red-headed looks like it's wearing a red hood with a black cape.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's a southern bird (the scientific name 'carolinus' refers to the Carolinas), the red-bellied woodpecker has been steadily expanding its range northward into New England over the past few decades, likely due to climate change and increased suburban bird feeding.
compareHints: Unlike its close relative the red-headed woodpecker, which has solid blocks of color (red head, black back, white belly), the red-bellied woodpecker shows a more complex pattern with its barred back and subtly colored underparts. Red-headed woodpeckers are much less common in New England and prefer more open habitats, while red-bellied woodpeckers readily adapt to suburban and wooded residential areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Within the Melanerpes genus, Red-headed Woodpeckers are easily distinguished from their cousin the Red-bellied Woodpecker by their solid black backs versus the Red-bellied's distinctive black-and-white barred pattern.
